paragraphs: “But I shall be told that he shammed illness on purpose, so that no one would suspect him, and that he told the prisoner about the money and the signals to tempt him into committing the murder. And then, when the prisoner had killed the old man and made off with the money, probably noisily enough to wake people, Smerdyakov got up—are we to believe this?—and went in. What for? To murder his master a second time and carry off money that was already stolen? Gentlemen, are you laughing? I am ashamed to put such suggestions to you. But incredible as it sounds, that is exactly what the prisoner alleges. He says that once he had left the house, knocked Grigory down and set off the alarm, Smerdyakov got up, went in, murdered his master and stole the money! I will not insist that Smerdyakov could hardly have counted on this in advance. He could hardly have foreseen that the furious, exasperated son, though he knew the signals, would merely peep in respectfully and then retreat, leaving Smerdyakov his booty. Gentlemen of the jury, I ask you in earnest: when could Smerdyakov have committed his crime? Name that moment, or you cannot accuse him.

“But perhaps the fit was real. The sick man suddenly came to himself, heard a shout, and went out. Well, and then? He looked around and said to himself, ‘Why not go and kill the master?’ And how would he have known what had happened, when he had lain unconscious until that moment? There is a limit to these flights of fancy.

“‘Very well,’ some shrewd people will say to me, ‘but suppose they were in agreement? Suppose they murdered him together and divided the money—what then?’ A weighty question, truly! And the facts behind it are astounding. One of them commits the murder and does all the work, while his accomplice lies to one side shamming a fit—evidently to rouse suspicion in everyone, and alarm in his master and in Grigory. I should like to know what motives could have led the two accomplices to hatch so insane a plan.

“Or perhaps Smerdyakov was no active accomplice, only a passive one. Perhaps he was cowed into agreeing not to prevent the murder. Foreseeing that he would be blamed for letting his master be killed without crying out or resisting, he may have obtained leave from Dmitri Karamazov to get out of the way by shamming a fit—‘you may murder him as you please; it is nothing to me.’ But this attack of Smerdyakov’s was bound to throw the whole household into confusion, so Dmitri Karamazov could never have agreed to such a plan. I will waive that point, however. Suppose he did agree. It would still follow that Dmitri Karamazov is the murderer and the instigator, and that Smerdyakov is only a passive accomplice—not even an accomplice, but a man who gave in against his will, out of terror.

“Yet what do we actually see? The moment he is arrested, the prisoner throws all the blame on Smerdyakov. He does not accuse him of being an accomplice; he accuses him of being the murderer himself. ‘He did it alone,’ he says. ‘He murdered and robbed him. It was the work of his hands.’ What odd accomplices, who start accusing each other at once! And think what a risk Karamazov ran. He commits the murder while his accomplice lies in bed, and then he puts the blame on the invalid. The invalid might well have resented that, and to save himself might well have confessed the truth. He might well have seen that the court would soon judge how far he was responsible, and might well have reckoned that his own punishment would be much lighter than the real murderer’s. In that case he would certainly have confessed. He has not. Smerdyakov never hinted at any complicity, though the actual murderer kept accusing him and insisting that he had done it alone.

“Moreover, Smerdyakov volunteered at the inquiry that it was _he_ who had told the prisoner about the envelope of notes and the signals, and that without him the prisoner would have known nothing of them. Had he really been a guilty accomplice, would he have admitted this so readily at the inquiry? Quite the opposite: he would have tried to hide it, to twist the facts or make little of them. But he did nothing of the kind. Only an innocent man, with no fear of being charged as an accomplice, could have behaved as he did. And then yesterday, in a fit of melancholy brought on by his illness and by this catastrophe, he hanged himself. He left a note in his peculiar language: ‘I destroy myself of my own will and inclination so as to throw no blame on any one.’ What would it have cost him to add: ‘I am the murderer, not Karamazov’? That he did not add. Are we to think that his conscience drove him to suicide but not to confessing his guilt?

“And what came next? Notes for three thousand roubles were brought into the court a short while ago. We were told that they were the same notes that lay in the envelope now on the table before us, and that the witness had received them from Smerdyakov the day before. I need not go back over that painful scene, but I will offer one or two comments, picking ones so small that they might escape notice at first glance and so be overlooked. First, Smerdyakov must have returned the money and hanged himself yesterday out of remorse. And only yesterday, as Ivan Karamazov tells us, he confessed his guilt to him. If that were not so, why would Ivan Fyodorovitch have stayed silent until now? And if Smerdyakov did confess, then I ask again: why did he not state the whole truth in the last letter he left behind, knowing that the innocent prisoner would face this terrible ordeal the next day?

“The money alone proves nothing. A week ago, quite by chance, I and two other persons in this court learned that Ivan Fyodorovitch had sent two five per cent. coupons, of five thousand each—ten thousand in all—to the chief town of the province to be exchanged. I mention it only to show that anyone may have money, and that there is no proving these notes to be the same ones that were in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s envelope.

“Yesterday Ivan Karamazov received a communication of the utmost importance from the real murderer, and did not stir. Why did he not report it at once? Why put it all off until the morning? I believe I have a right to guess why. His health had been failing for a week. He had admitted to a doctor and to his closest friends that he suffered from hallucinations and saw phantoms of the dead. He was on the eve of the brain fever that has laid him low today. In that state he suddenly heard that Smerdyakov was dead, and at once thought, ‘The man is dead; I can put the blame on him and save my brother. I have money. I will take a roll of notes and say that Smerdyakov gave them to me before he died.’ You will say that this was dishonorable: it is dishonorable to slander even the dead, even to save a brother. True. But what if he slandered him without knowing it? What if, finally unhinged by the sudden news of the valet’s death, he imagined it really was so? You saw the scene just now. You have seen the state the witness was in. He stood there and spoke, but where was his mind?

“Then came the document: the prisoner’s letter, written two days before the crime, which lays out a complete program of the murder. Why, then, should we look for any other program? The crime was carried out exactly according to this one, and by none other than the man who wrote it. Yes, gentlemen of the jury, it went off without a hitch! He did not run away humbly and timidly from his father’s window, although he was firmly convinced that the object of his affections was in there with the old man. No, that is absurd and improbable! He went in and murdered him. Most likely he killed him in a rage, burning with resentment, the moment he laid eyes on his hated rival. But having killed him, probably with a single blow of the brass pestle, and having searched carefully and made sure that she was not there, he still remembered to slide his hand under the pillow and take out the envelope. Its torn cover lies now on the table before us.

“I mention this so that you may notice one circumstance which seems to me very characteristic. Suppose he had been an experienced murderer, killing only for gain. Would he have left the torn envelope on the floor, where it was found, beside the corpse? Take Smerdyakov, for instance, murdering his master to rob him. He would simply have carried the envelope off. He would not have bothered to open it over his victim’s body, since he knew for certain that the notes were inside—they had been put in and sealed in his presence—and if he had taken the envelope with him, no one would ever have known there had been a robbery. I ask you, gentlemen, would Smerdyakov have acted in that way? Would he have left the envelope on the floor?

“No. This was the act of a frantic murderer, a murderer who was no thief and had never stolen anything before that day. He snatched the notes from under the pillow, not like a thief taking them, but as if he were seizing his own property back from the thief who had stolen it. For that was the idea that had grown into an almost insane obsession in Dmitri Karamazov about that money. He pounced on the envelope, which he had never seen before, and tore it open to make sure the money was inside. Then he ran off with the money in his pocket, never stopping to consider that he had left an astounding piece of evidence against himself in that torn envelope on the floor. All because it was Karamazov and not Smerdyakov: he did not think, he did not reflect, and how could he? He ran; he heard the servant cry out behind him; the old man seized him, tried to stop him, and was struck down by the brass pestle.

“The prisoner, moved by pity, leapt down to look at him. Would you believe it, he tells us that he leapt down out of pity, out of compassion, to see whether he could do anything for the man. Was that a moment for compassion? No. He jumped down only to make certain whether the one witness of his crime was dead or alive. Any other feeling, any other motive, would be unnatural. Note that he took pains over Grigory: he wiped his head with his handkerchief, and, satisfied that Grigory was dead, ran to his mistress’s house, dazed and covered with blood. How did it never occur to him that he was covered with blood and would be caught at once? But the prisoner himself assures us that he did not even notice the blood. That may be believed; it is quite possible; it always happens to criminals at such moments. On one point they show diabolical cunning, while on another they miss everything. But at that moment he was thinking of one thing only—where was _she_? He wanted to find out at once where she was, so he ran to her lodging and learned an unexpected and astounding piece of news: she had gone off to Mokroe to meet her first lover.”
